items.title: Level 2: Why the baseline checks exist
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Government holds a great deal of information about people and about how the country is run. It also controls buildings, systems and money. The Baseline Personnel Security Standard, or BPSS, exists so that departments can give people access to these things with reasonable confidence. It reduces the risk that someone joins under a false name, is not allowed to work in the UK, hides a work history that matters, or has an unspent conviction that makes the role unsuitable. The BPSS is not a security clearance. It is a package of pre-employment checks that covers four main areas: your identity, your nationality and immigration status, your employment history, and your criminal record. Because it is the baseline, it applies to everybody who joins the Civil Service, from the most junior new starter to a senior leader. Contractors and people on temporary work in government usually need it as well. Passing the BPSS does not give you access to secret information. It only shows that you have met the minimum standard. Some roles then need a security clearance on top. The same principles apply at every level: be open, give accurate answers and keep copies of what you send. The checks protect the public, the department and you.

questions.prompt: How is the BPSS best described?

options.text: A single form that is filled in once and then never checked
A package of pre-employment checks that is not itself a clearance
A civil service qualification awarded after a short course
The lowest of the formal security clearances, sitting just below CTC

questions.hint: The BPSS is a set of pre-employment checks rather than a security clearance.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the four main areas covered by the BPSS?

options.text: Medical history
Education history
Credit history
Employment history

questions.hint: Identity, nationality and immigration status, employment history and criminal record are the four areas.

questions.prompt: Who has to meet the BPSS?

options.text: Only people working in the security services or other sensitive areas
Only people who have recently lived abroad
Everyone joining the Civil Service, at every grade
Only people applying for senior roles with access to sensitive material

questions.hint: It is the baseline, so it applies to all new joiners.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason government uses baseline checks?

options.text: To decide which grade a new starter should be placed in
To give people access to information and systems with reasonable confidence
To make sure only people from certain backgrounds are allowed to apply for jobs
To test whether candidates hold the exact qualifications that the advert asked for

questions.hint: The checks reduce risk before access is given.

questions.prompt: Which risk is the identity check mainly designed to reduce?

options.text: Someone claiming expenses they are not owed
Someone joining under a false name
Someone joining the wrong team by mistake
Someone sharing passwords with a colleague

questions.hint: Proving who you are guards against false identities.

questions.prompt: What does passing the BPSS tell the department?

options.text: You have been placed on a waiting list for CTC
You have met the minimum standard, which does not open secret material
You may now see secret information once your manager has agreed it
You are entitled to a higher pay band than people who have not been checked

questions.hint: BPSS is a minimum standard and does not by itself open access to secret material.

questions.prompt: How are contractors and temporary workers in government usually treated?

options.text: They need the checks only if they are paid at a higher rate than permanent staff
They are exempt from checks, because they only work for a short time in government
They are covered if their agency has met its own checks
They usually need baseline checks too, because they can access the same things

questions.hint: Anyone with access to government assets is usually checked.

questions.prompt: Which principle applies to checks at every level?

options.text: Give details only if they are asked for twice
Give short answers to keep the forms simple
Give the information to your manager, not the checks team
Give accurate answers and be open about your history

questions.hint: Accuracy and openness underpin every level of checking.

items.title: Level 2: Documents and who checks them
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: The department checks that your identity documents are genuine as well as asking to see them. The reason is simple: false documents are one of the main ways in which people try to get into jobs they should not have. Originals are usually required because copies are easy to change. Staff who check documents are trained to look at features like the photograph, the dates, the spelling of names and any security features. Where the documents allow it, the department may also confirm them with the body that issued them. You are usually asked for a mixture of document types. Some show who you are, such as a passport or photocard driving licence. Others show where you live, such as a recent bank statement, a council tax letter or a utility bill. Some departments also ask for a National Insurance number, which is used for tax and National Insurance contributions. The name and address on your documents should be consistent. If they are not, for example because you have recently moved, explain why when you send them. Documents must be current and not out of date unless the instructions say otherwise. Do not send documents by ordinary email unless the department asks for that, and use the secure route it provides. Keep your originals safe because you may need them for other purposes.

questions.prompt: Why does the department usually ask for originals rather than copies?

options.text: Copies are easier to alter than originals
Originals are easier to scan into the system
Originals are required by law for UK citizens only
Originals are cheaper to store than copies

questions.hint: Alteration of copies is the main reason for asking for originals.

questions.prompt: What might trained staff look at when checking a document?

options.text: The photograph, the dates and the spelling of names
The size of the document, which must match a standard
The age of the document, which must be under a year old
The signature, which must be in black ink

questions.hint: They examine details that show a document is genuine.

questions.prompt: Which document is a typical example of one that shows where you live?

options.text: A photocard driving licence
A birth certificate
A passport
A recent bank statement

questions.hint: Statements and bills show your address; passports and licences mainly prove identity.

questions.prompt: Which pair is a sensible mix of document types?

options.text: A bank statement and a council tax letter only
Two copies of the same utility bill, sent in separate emails
A passport and a second passport from the same country
A passport for identity and a bank statement for address

questions.hint: A mixture shows both who you are and where you live.

questions.prompt: What is a National Insurance number mainly used for?

options.text: Tax and National Insurance contributions
Booking annual leave through the HR system
Applying for the right level of security clearance
Entering your new workplace on the first day

questions.hint: The number is used by HMRC and for contributions.

questions.prompt: What should you do if the address on one document differs because you recently moved?

options.text: Change the older document yourself
Send only the document that has the newest address
Explain the difference when you send them
Wait for the department to notice and ask

questions.hint: A short explanation avoids confusion and delay.

questions.prompt: How should you send your documents?

options.text: By ordinary email, since it is quickest
By posting them with no tracking
By asking a friend who works there to hand them in
By the secure route the department provides

questions.hint: Use the secure method named by the department.

questions.prompt: Why are current documents usually asked for rather than out-of-date ones?

options.text: Out-of-date documents are not accepted in any country
Out-of-date documents may not show who you are now
Current documents are only needed for managers
Current documents are cheaper for the department to scan

questions.hint: Current documents reflect your present situation.

items.title: Level 2: Self-employment and other histories
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: The employment history check looks at what you were doing in the recent past, normally the last three years. Not everyone has a simple list of employers. If you were self-employed, you can describe the work you did and name people who can confirm it, such as customers, a business partner or an accountant. If you did agency or temporary work, list the agency and the places you worked if you can. If you were studying, name the school, college or university and the dates. If you were claiming benefits or looking for work, a job centre adviser or other official may be able to confirm that. If you travelled or lived abroad, say where and for how long, and explain what you did. Caring for a child or a relative is a valid reason too. The key point is that the whole period should be accounted for, and that your account is true. Departments often ask for referees who know you in a professional or personal capacity, but they can also look at contact details in your records. If you cannot trace a former employer, for example because the business closed, say so and offer another way to confirm what you did. Never make up a person or a business to fill a gap. It is much better to explain a real situation honestly than to hide it.

questions.prompt: What period does the employment history check usually cover?

options.text: The last three years
The last ten years
The last three months
Only your current job

questions.hint: The standard period for the history check is three years.

questions.prompt: If you were self-employed, who could help confirm your work?

options.text: A former school teacher
Customers, a business partner or an accountant
Only your bank manager
Only a close relative who has lived with you throughout

questions.hint: People who dealt with you in business can confirm what you did.

questions.prompt: What would you give for a period of study?

options.text: A copy of your final grade only
A list of the books and papers that you read during the course
The name of the school, college or university and the dates
The name of a friend who studied with you

questions.hint: Name and dates let the department confirm that you studied.

questions.prompt: Who might be able to confirm a period of looking for work?

options.text: A job centre adviser
A letting agent
A local councillor
A recruitment website owner

questions.hint: A job centre adviser can usually confirm job-seeking.

questions.prompt: You lived abroad for part of the period. What should you do?

options.text: Leave it out, because the check only covers time spent in the UK
Say you were on holiday for the whole time
Give the dates of your last UK job instead
Say where and for how long, and explain what you did

questions.hint: Time abroad should be accounted for too.

questions.prompt: Your previous employer has closed down. What is the best approach?

options.text: Wait until the department asks about it
Name another employer that is still open and has similar work
Leave the job off the form
Say so and offer another way to confirm what you did

questions.hint: Offer another route for confirmation rather than skipping it.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the history check is correct?

options.text: Gaps in work are acceptable, but they must always be left blank on the form
The whole period should be accounted for and the account should be true
Short gaps never need to be explained, even if they come to light later
Only gaps of more than a year matter, and shorter ones can be skipped

questions.hint: Departments want a complete and truthful account.

questions.prompt: How is caring for a child or relative treated as an explanation for time out of paid work?

options.text: As a reason that only counts if you received an allowance
As a reason that is not accepted for the history check
As a reason that is accepted only for a close relative
As a genuine reason, if you describe it honestly

questions.hint: Caring is a genuine and accepted explanation.

items.title: Level 2: Declaring convictions
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: The criminal record part of the BPSS asks about unspent convictions. The law on spent and unspent convictions is called rehabilitation. It recognises that people can move on from offences after a period of time. How long that period is depends on the sentence given, not the offence alone, and different rules apply across the UK. For that reason you should not guess. Ask the checks team or an advice service if you are unsure. When you fill in the form, you will usually be asked to declare any unspent convictions. Some posts, especially in security, justice or policing, are exempt from the usual rules, which means you may be asked about spent convictions too. The advert or form will say if this applies. The department then usually checks your answers with the official records service for the part of the UK where you live, for example through a basic disclosure certificate. Having an unspent conviction does not automatically stop you being appointed. The department considers factors such as how serious the offence was, how long ago it happened, how you have behaved since and whether it relates to the job. If you declare it honestly, the department can consider the whole picture. If you hide it and the check finds it, the department may conclude that you cannot be trusted and withdraw the offer.

questions.prompt: Which kind of conviction does the criminal record part of the BPSS ask about?

options.text: Convictions of any age, spent or unspent
Convictions from outside the UK only
Convictions for driving offences only
Unspent convictions

questions.hint: The BPSS asks about unspent convictions.

questions.prompt: What does the time before a conviction becomes spent depend on?

options.text: The sentence given
The job the person applies for
The age of the person at interview
The department that checks it

questions.hint: The sentence determines how long the conviction takes to become spent.

questions.prompt: Why should you not simply guess whether a conviction is spent?

options.text: Guessing is treated as a criminal offence
Spent convictions are never relevant to any job
Rules vary across the UK, so it is easy to get wrong
The department will not accept an answer without legal advice

questions.hint: Rules vary, so check rather than assume.

questions.prompt: Why might some posts ask about spent convictions as well?

options.text: They are the most senior posts in each department and have wider powers
They are posts open only to long-serving staff
They are exempt from the usual rules because of the work involved
They are posts based in central government buildings in London only

questions.hint: Exempt posts, such as some in policing or justice, are allowed to ask.

questions.prompt: How does the department usually check what you declare?

options.text: Through the official records service for the part of the UK where you live
By asking your referees to confirm that your declaration is complete
By searching your social media pages for any mention of an offence
By contacting your neighbours and former landlords about you

questions.hint: Official records services provide criminal record certificates.

questions.prompt: Which factor might the department weigh up about an unspent conviction?

options.text: Whether your family have also been convicted
How long ago it happened and how it relates to the job
Whether you have paid the court costs early
Whether you have told your colleagues about it

questions.hint: The department weighs the seriousness, age and relevance of the offence.

questions.prompt: What may happen if you hide a conviction and the check finds it?

options.text: The department may decide you cannot be trusted and withdraw the offer
The department will add a note and take no further action
The department will delay your start by a month
The department will ask you to repeat the check

questions.hint: Concealing a conviction damages trust more than declaring it would.

questions.prompt: How can declaring a conviction honestly help you?

options.text: It makes the conviction spent straight away
It guarantees that the offer will be confirmed
It lets the department consider the whole picture
It means the check will not be carried out

questions.hint: Honesty allows a fair assessment of your situation.

items.title: Level 2: Right to work for different people
items.body: Everybody who works for an employer in the UK must have the right to work here, and employers must check it before the worker starts. How you prove it depends on your status. British citizens can usually prove it with a British passport or a certificate of registration or naturalisation, or other documents shown on the official list. Irish citizens have long had the right to live and work in the UK, and can prove it with an Irish passport or passport card. People from other countries have the right to work only if their immigration status allows it. This could be settled status, indefinite leave to remain, or a visa that permits work. Some people can show their status through an online Home Office check, using a share code that they create in their online account. Employers must check the documents are genuine, belong to you and are still valid, and they must keep a copy. If your permission to work has an end date, your employer will check again before it ends. It is your responsibility to keep your status up to date and to tell your employer of any change in good time. Having the right to work is a separate matter from the nationality rules for individual Civil Service jobs, which are explained in each advert.

questions.prompt: When must an employer check a worker's right to work?

options.text: Only if the worker asks for it
Within the first year
Only if there is a complaint
Before the worker starts

questions.hint: The check must happen before employment begins.

questions.prompt: Which of these can a British citizen use to prove the right to work?

options.text: A council tax letter
A bank statement
A British passport
A reference letter

questions.hint: A British passport is a standard proof for British citizens.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Irish citizens is correct?

options.text: They cannot work in public sector jobs
They can only work in Northern Ireland
They have long had the right to live and work in the UK
They always need a work visa, as they are not UK nationals

questions.hint: Irish citizens have an established right to work in the UK.

questions.prompt: What does the right to work of someone from another country depend on?

options.text: Whether their immigration status allows work
Whether they hold a UK bank account
Whether their employer pays a fee to the Home Office
Whether they speak English at home or with their family

questions.hint: Immigration status determines permission to work.

questions.prompt: What is a share code used for?

options.text: To get access to a staff car park or a similar facility
To let an employer check your status in an online Home Office check
To share your wages between two bank accounts
To share your training notes with colleagues

questions.hint: It enables an online check of right to work.

questions.prompt: What must an employer do with the documents it checks?

options.text: Post the originals to the Home Office for a second check
Return them to you straight away and keep no record at all
Share them with other employers who ask
Check they are genuine and valid, and keep a copy

questions.hint: Employers keep a copy as a record of the check.

questions.prompt: What happens if someone's permission to work has an end date?

options.text: The employer will check again before it ends
The contract continues without any further checks
The employer cannot check again until the date passes
The person must leave on the date, without notice

questions.hint: Time-limited permission leads to a follow-up check.

questions.prompt: Whose responsibility is it to keep your status up to date?

options.text: Your line manager's, who will chase it each year
The Home Office's alone, which will tell the employer
Yours, and you should tell your employer of changes in good time
Your bank's, which will tell the employer

questions.hint: You are responsible for telling your employer.

items.title: Level 2: Nationality rules for particular jobs
items.body: The right to work and nationality rules are two separate things. The right to work is a legal question that applies to every employer. The Civil Service also has nationality rules, which decide who may be appointed to which jobs. The rules apply to the job, not to the person as an individual. In general, many Civil Service jobs are open to UK nationals and also to citizens of some other countries, such as Commonwealth and Irish citizens, and to people with certain immigration permissions, subject to conditions. Some jobs are reserved for UK nationals only. These are typically jobs where the work is closely linked to national security, defence or the intelligence agencies. Every advert states which group of people can apply, usually in a short eligibility statement. Different departments and roles can have different rules, so you should read each one. If you hold more than one nationality, this does not usually prevent you applying for general jobs, but for reserved posts the position is more specific, and the advert or the recruitment team can explain. Do not rely on rules you have heard from friends, since they can change. When in doubt, ask the recruitment contact before you apply. Giving wrong information about your nationality or status on a form is treated very seriously.

questions.prompt: What do the Civil Service nationality rules decide?

options.text: Which jobs different people may be appointed to
Which exams different people must pass
Where different people may be based
How much different people are paid for the same job

questions.hint: The rules decide who is eligible for which jobs.

questions.prompt: To what do the nationality rules attach?

options.text: The job, not the person as an individual
The person's age when they apply for the job
The person's previous employer
The person's home town or the part of the UK they live in

questions.hint: The rules are attached to the job.

questions.prompt: Which type of job is typically reserved for UK nationals only?

options.text: Work in finance teams that deal with large budgets
Work closely linked to national security or the intelligence agencies
Work in a contact centre handling calls from the public
Work in departments outside London and the South East

questions.hint: National security roles are the usual reserved posts.

questions.prompt: Where does an advert say who can apply?

options.text: In its closing date and application instructions
In its job title and summary at the top
In its pay scale and grade details
In its eligibility statement

questions.hint: The eligibility statement lists who can apply.

questions.prompt: How do nationality rules compare between departments and roles?

options.text: They differ only between London and the regions
They are identical everywhere
Different roles can have different rules
They differ only between full-time and part-time jobs

questions.hint: Rules can vary by department and role.

questions.prompt: You hold dual nationality and see a reserved post. What is sensible?

options.text: Apply without reading and see what happens
Read the advert carefully and ask the recruitment team
List only the nationality that suits you
Assume you are not eligible and skip it

questions.hint: Reserved posts have specific positions, so ask.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to rely on rules you have heard from friends?

options.text: Friends are not allowed to talk about the Civil Service
Rules can change and your own position may differ
The rules are the same for everyone
Friends may be required to report you

questions.hint: Rules change and apply to your own status.

questions.prompt: How seriously is wrong information about your nationality or status treated?

options.text: As a matter only for your referee
Very seriously, and it can end the process
As a matter for your first review
As a small matter if you correct it at interview

questions.hint: Misstatements damage trust and can end your application.

items.title: Level 2: What clearance is for
items.body: Security clearance is the next step above the baseline checks for roles where the work is more sensitive. It is about trust and risk. The aim of vetting is to judge whether a person could be at risk of being pressured, tempted or tricked into harming national security, and whether they are reliable and honest. The assessment looks at your background, your behaviour and your circumstances. It is not a judgement on you as a person, and it does not look for perfection. Clearance is linked to a particular role. Someone has a clearance because their job needs it, and an employer cannot ask for a higher level than the role requires. Three points are worth knowing. First, the sponsoring department starts the process, and you cannot apply for it on your own. Second, clearance takes time, and for some levels it can take months, which is why jobs that need it often say you can only start when it is granted. Third, clearance does not last forever. It is reviewed after a period, and you may be asked to complete new forms. Holding clearance also carries responsibilities, such as reporting important changes in your circumstances. These could include a new partner from abroad or a serious change in your finances. If you tell the security team early, they can usually help.

questions.prompt: What is security clearance mainly about?

options.text: Fitness and health
Experience and qualifications
Speed and efficiency
Trust and risk

questions.hint: Clearance judges whether a person can be trusted with sensitive work.

questions.prompt: What does vetting try to judge?

options.text: Whether you have enough experience for the next grade
Whether you could be pressured or tricked into harming national security
Whether you are the strongest candidate at interview
Whether you would be a good manager of other people in the future

questions.hint: Vetting assesses risk to national security and reliability.

questions.prompt: How should vetting be understood?

options.text: As an assessment of risk for a particular role, not of your worth
As a ranking of your personality against others
As a test of how well you know the law
As a test that only managers must take

questions.hint: It looks at risk and reliability, not worth as a person.

questions.prompt: Why does an employer not ask for a higher level of clearance than needed?

options.text: Higher levels are not allowed in the Civil Service
Higher levels are only given to contractors
Clearance is linked to what the role requires
Higher levels cost the candidate money

questions.hint: Clearance matches the sensitivity of the role.

questions.prompt: Who starts the clearance process?

options.text: The candidate, once they have been made an offer
The candidate's referee
The sponsoring department
The candidate's bank

questions.hint: The department asks for clearance on your behalf.

questions.prompt: Why do some jobs say you can only start once clearance is granted?

options.text: Clearance can be done in a day but is only carried out on certain dates
Clearance is a type of probation that runs alongside your first months
Clearance is only needed after the first year, once you have settled in
Clearance can take months and access cannot be given before it is in place

questions.hint: Access cannot be given until clearance is in place.

questions.prompt: How long does clearance last?

options.text: It lasts for life once granted, whichever job you move to
It is reviewed after a period and may need renewing
It ends each year on your start date unless the department renews it
It ends each time you change team and has to be started again

questions.hint: Clearance is reviewed and may need renewing.

questions.prompt: Which change might you need to report to the security team once you are cleared?

options.text: A serious change in your finances or a new partner from abroad
A change in your working pattern that moves you to part-time hours
A change of GP surgery or dentist in a new area
A change in your travel route to work

questions.hint: Important changes in circumstances should be reported early.

items.title: Level 2: How government information is marked
items.body: Government marks its information according to how damaging it could be if it were lost or shared by mistake. Under the Government Security Classifications Policy there are three levels: OFFICIAL, SECRET and TOP SECRET. Most government information is OFFICIAL. This covers the day-to-day business of departments, such as emails, policy papers and customer records. Even OFFICIAL information must be looked after properly, and some of it is more sensitive than the rest. That information can carry an extra handling marker, OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE. This is not a separate level, but a reminder to take extra care. SECRET information is more sensitive, and loss or disclosure could seriously harm the work of government or national security. TOP SECRET is the most sensitive of all, and its loss could cause exceptionally grave damage. The classification matters for your career because it influences the clearance level a job needs. Most roles that handle only OFFICIAL information need only the baseline checks. Jobs that regularly handle SECRET material usually need a Security Check, and jobs with extensive access to TOP SECRET material usually need Developed Vetting. As a new starter you should learn how your department marks and shares information. If you receive something that looks wrongly marked, or you are not sure how to handle it, ask your line manager or the security team before you act.

Six
Three
Four

options.text: CONFIDENTIAL
OFFICIAL
SECRET

options.text: A label used only for information from abroad
A name for a type of security pass
A handling marker for OFFICIAL information needing extra care
A fourth classification level above OFFICIAL

questions.prompt: Which level is the most sensitive?

options.text: OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE
SECRET
OFFICIAL
TOP SECRET

questions.hint: TOP SECRET is the highest classification.

questions.prompt: How do classifications connect to clearance?

options.text: They decide the salary and grade of the job you do
They decide how many days of leave you get
They decide which building and floor you work in
They influence the level of clearance a job needs

questions.hint: Higher classifications generally need higher clearance.

questions.prompt: What clearance does a job that regularly handles SECRET material usually need?

options.text: A basic criminal record check only
Developed Vetting only
Security Check
Baseline checks only

questions.hint: SC usually goes with regular access to SECRET assets.

questions.prompt: What clearance do jobs with extensive access to TOP SECRET material usually need?

options.text: Counter-Terrorist Check
Baseline checks only
Security Check only
Developed Vetting

questions.hint: DV typically goes with extensive access to TOP SECRET.

questions.prompt: You are not sure how to handle some information. What is the best step?

options.text: Ask your line manager or the security team before acting
Send it to a friend who works in IT for advice

questions.hint: Ask before you act if you are unsure.

items.title: Level 2: CTC and SC
items.body: Two of the clearance levels above the baseline are the Counter-Terrorist Check, or CTC, and the Security Check, or SC. The CTC is for roles where the work places you near people or sites that could be targeted by terrorism, or where you have some access to sensitive material. Examples include certain roles near public figures or at sensitive buildings. It includes the baseline checks, plus checks of security and intelligence records, and the sponsor decides whether the role really needs it. The Security Check, or SC, is a step up. It is for roles that regularly handle SECRET material, or that involve frequent access to sensitive sites. As well as the baseline checks, SC involves a deeper look at your background. This can include a credit reference check, which is a way of seeing how you manage money, and checks on records held by the security services. You complete a security questionnaire that asks about where you have lived, your work and your close family. A minimum period of residence in the UK normally applies, and the advert will say if so. Not every gap or past difficulty means failure. The vetting team look at the overall picture, such as how you have handled problems and whether you have been open. Both levels take longer than the baseline. SC in particular can take months.

questions.prompt: What do the letters CTC stand for in a job advert?

options.text: Civil Team Clearance
Council Tax Check
Central Training Certificate
Counter-Terrorist Check

questions.hint: CTC is the Counter-Terrorist Check.

questions.prompt: What kind of work might need a CTC?

options.text: Roles near people or sites that could be targeted by terrorism
Roles with no access to anything sensitive or restricted at all
Roles in learning and development teams
Every office job in the Civil Service

questions.hint: CTC links to terrorism risk and some access to sensitive material.

questions.prompt: Which kind of work usually needs an SC?

options.text: Handling only public information leaflets
Regularly handling SECRET material
Booking rooms and ordering stationery
Taking calls from members of the public

questions.hint: SC links to regular access to SECRET material.

questions.prompt: What does a credit reference check show?

options.text: How you manage credit and money
How often you have moved house
How well you did at school
How many jobs you have held

questions.hint: It shows your financial history and how you manage credit.

questions.prompt: What is a typical part of the SC process?

options.text: Completing a detailed security questionnaire about your background
Sitting a written exam on current affairs and the law

items.title: Level 2: Developed Vetting
items.body: Developed Vetting, or DV, is the highest level of personnel security clearance. It is used for roles with frequent and extensive access to TOP SECRET material, or for certain posts in the security and intelligence agencies. It is very rare in entry-level Administrative Officer jobs, but it is useful to understand what it involves. DV includes the baseline checks and the checks done for SC, and then goes much further. The vetting team look at your finances in more detail. Interviews are carried out with you, and with referees who know you well and are asked about your character and reliability. Your circumstances are examined over a longer period. A longer period of UK residence is usually expected than for lower levels, though the exact requirement depends on the role, and the advert should say so. Because so much is involved, DV can take longer than any of the other levels, often many months. Clearance at this level is reviewed after a period and holders are expected to report changes in their lives, such as a new relationship, a significant financial change or contact with certain people. Staff with DV also take part in what is called aftercare, which is regular support and monitoring that helps keep the clearance valid. As with every level, being open from the start is the best way to avoid problems.

items.title: Level 2: Steps in the vetting process
items.body: If your role needs clearance above the baseline, the process follows a series of steps. First, the sponsoring department confirms the level the role needs and asks United Kingdom Security Vetting, or UKSV, to begin. Second, you are invited to complete a security questionnaire, usually online. You should answer fully and honestly, keep a copy, and ask the department security team if you do not understand a question. Third, UKSV carries out checks. These can include criminal records, security service records and, at higher levels, financial checks. Fourth, for some levels, referees are contacted and an interview may be held. Fifth, a decision is made about whether to grant clearance. Sometimes more information is needed, and you may be contacted to explain something. The outcome is passed to your sponsoring department and you are told the result. If clearance is refused, there is an appeal route and you may ask for the decision to be reviewed. A refusal for one role does not necessarily mean you cannot get a different kind of job in government, as many do not need clearance. After clearance is granted, there is aftercare, which means you keep the department informed of changes in your life and the clearance is reviewed from time to time. Throughout, your information is handled confidentially and used only for vetting.

items.title: Level 2: Money and honesty in vetting
items.body: At higher levels of clearance, vetting looks at your finances. This surprises some people, who worry that any debt means failure. That is not the case. The reason for looking at money is that serious financial difficulty, or hidden financial problems, can make a person open to pressure or temptation. Vetting teams are interested in whether you manage your money responsibly and whether you are honest about it. Ordinary borrowing, such as a mortgage, a car loan or a credit card, is normal. What can cause concern is a history of unpaid debts that you have ignored, large debts you cannot explain, or gambling that has got out of control. If you are struggling, it is usually better to seek advice and make a plan to repay before you apply. Free debt advice is available from independent charities. When you fill in the questionnaire, declare the information that is asked for, and give an account that matches what the credit check will show. Differences between your answers and the record can raise questions. The same applies to other areas of life such as drug use, past conduct or contact with people overseas: vetting does not look for a perfect past but for honesty and reliability. Trying to hide a problem is nearly always worse than the problem itself.

items.title: Level 2: Pay, tax and pension for new starters
items.body: When you join the Civil Service, there are some practical matters to sort out in the first weeks. You are usually paid monthly, directly into your bank account, so you will need to give your bank details to the payroll team. You will also be asked for your National Insurance number and some tax information. In many cases you complete a starter checklist so that HMRC can give you the right tax code. If you have been working elsewhere, you may need a leaving document from your last job, such as a P45, to help the payroll set up your tax correctly. Check your first payslip carefully to make sure the amount and the tax code look right, and raise any problem with the payroll team early. Most new civil servants are automatically enrolled in a Civil Service pension scheme, and part of your pay is paid into it. This is a valuable benefit, and the department will explain the details. You can usually opt out, but it is worth reading the guidance before you decide. You will also learn about your leave entitlement and how to book time off. Keep copies of your contract, payslips and pension papers in a safe place. If you do not understand something, the HR or payroll helpdesk can explain.

items.title: Level 2: Your first weeks and the Civil Service Code
items.body: The Civil Service Code sets out the values that civil servants are expected to follow. There are four: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Integrity means putting the obligations of public service above your own interests. Honesty means being truthful and open. Objectivity means basing your advice and decisions on rigorous analysis of the evidence. Impartiality means acting solely according to the merits of the case and serving equally well governments of different political persuasions. As a new starter, these values affect everyday things. You must not use your position for personal gain. You should declare any interest that could look like a conflict, for example if a friend or relative applies for something your team decides. You should not accept gifts or hospitality that could influence you, and you should check your department's rules. You are expected to keep official information confidential, including when you are outside work. You also need to be careful about what you post on social media, particularly about political matters, so that you remain trusted as impartial. If you see something wrong, such as fraud or a breach of the Code, you can raise it with your line manager or through other routes your department provides, and you should not be punished for doing so honestly. Your induction and mandatory learning will explain how these values work in your department.
